w: 1 McGuire & Nunn order: good, fair, poor, questionable, hopeless A professor's hint · 2 questions in the bank Know this The in-class poll questions (McGuire & Nunn's driving factor, its accuracy, category order, diagnostic vs. therapeutic) are signaled as midterm material. Know that McGuire & Nunn sorts by maintainability, its ~80% / ~50% accuracy figures, and the exact category order. In McGuire & Nunn, questionable comes after poor. A questionable tooth either gets worse (hopeless) or improves (poor). The in-person session (a Slido review, which Dr. Geisinger said "might inform the midterm") was about telling the three prognosis systems apart by what each one is based on, not by memorizing lists. McGuire & Nunn sorts teeth by whether they can be maintained, meaning kept in the mouth. Most of the class guessed "disease progression" and was wrong. Its order is good → fair → poor → questionable → hopeless, and the classic mistake is swapping poor and questionable. Poor teeth (attachment loss, Class II furcation, mobility) can be kept with significant effort. A questionable tooth is one we genuinely question keeping, and it does not stay there: it gets worse and becomes hopeless, or it improves and moves up to poor. 2 McGuire & Nunn rates retention (maintainability); about 80% / 50% accurate A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this McGuire & Nunn is about tooth retention (diagnostic or therapeutic). Kwok & Caton is about periodontal stability (therapeutic only), which is why questionable sits in its middle. Only McGuire & Nunn works as a diagnostic prognosis. Any of the three can be used therapeutically. How accurate is it? All of the poll statements were true. It is right about 80% of the time overall (81% at 8 years). Once the good teeth are taken out of the analysis, it drops to about 50%, a coin flip. On average, teeth do better than predicted, and even hopeless teeth in well-maintained patients are often kept much longer than expected. The exceptions are smokers and patients with very poor hygiene, and even very poor hygiene tracks the prediction if those patients keep up with maintenance. Most teeth leave the mouth because a dentist extracts them, not because they exfoliate (unlike implants). McGuire & Nunn can be given per tooth or for the whole dentition, and as a diagnostic prognosis (what happens if the patient takes no treatment) or a therapeutic prognosis (how the recommended treatment changes the outcome). The therapeutic version is a good way to show a patient what treatment buys them. Kwok & Caton asks whether periodontal stability (arrested attachment loss) can be achieved with treatment: likely, don't know, or unlikely. That is why questionable sits in its middle, and why it can only ever be therapeutic. It is the better choice for a medically complex patient, because smoking or vaping cessation and referral to get an A1c under control become part of the treatment it is judging. Miller & McEntire was studied only on molars. It is quantitative (A1c, smoking and other factors get numbers), and because it was built from patients who received 30 years of treatment and maintenance, it is therapeutic too. Smoking is its biggest single risk factor: about 296% more likely to lose those molars. The one-line summary: only McGuire & Nunn can be diagnostic; all three can be therapeutic. 3 Diagnostic vs therapeutic: only McGuire & Nunn works diagnostically A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Explained under 2 above: McGuire & Nunn rates retention (maintainability); about 80% / 50% accurate 4 Kwok & Caton (stability, whole dentition) and Miller & McEntire (molars) A professor's hint · 8 questions in the bank Explained under 2 above: McGuire & Nunn rates retention (maintainability); about 80% / 50% accurate 5 Risk-stratified maintenance intervals Core of the lecture · 5 questions in the bank Low risk — comprehensive periodontal exam every 6–12 months, radiographs every 12–24 months, professional biofilm/calculus removal every 6 months, standard home care (twice-daily brushing, once-daily interdental cleaning), nutrition counseling, tobacco-use prevention. High risk — comprehensive exam every 6–12 months plus screening every 3 months, radiographs every 6 months, close systemic monitoring with medical consults as needed, biofilm/calculus removal and subgingival debridement every 2–4 months, consideration of systemic or local adjunctive antimicrobials, surgical treatment likely necessary, and the same home-care/cessation/adjunct/compliance package as moderate risk, just monitored more tightly. Tooth loss occurs about twice as often in treated-but-non-maintained patients versus treated-and-maintained patients, and more frequent maintenance visits correlate with fewer teeth lost over time — yet patient compliance with maintenance runs only about 30–40%. The standard 3-month interval isn't arbitrary: pathogenic subgingival species begin re-establishing within 4–8 weeks of treatment, and by 9–11 weeks the subgingival microbiome can repopulate close to pre-treatment levels — a 3-month recall sits inside that window. Patients undergoing active orthodontic tooth movement are seen more often still (roughly every 4–6 weeks), both because that's when appliances are adjusted and because inflammation during active tooth movement can uncouple bone formation from bone resorption, risking real bone loss if biofilm isn't controlled tightly during that period. Regularity of maintenance, not just total quantity of visits, is what predicts tooth-loss risk, and that effect is larger for Stage 3/4 and Grade C patients — a patient at that severity who skips more than a year of maintenance across a 5-year window has roughly 2.5x the odds of losing a tooth to periodontitis compared to one who stays regular.
